paragraphs: Opinions in Leading Them to Concentrate Political Power

If it is true that in ages of equality men readily adopt the idea of a great central power, it cannot be doubted that their habits and feelings also predispose them to recognize such a power and to support it. This can be shown in a few words, because most of the reasons behind the fact have already been stated. *a Men who live in democratic countries have no superiors, no inferiors and no habitual or necessary partners in their undertakings. They readily fall back on themselves and regard themselves as beings apart. I had occasion to point this out at considerable length when I treated of individualism. Such men can therefore never tear themselves from their private affairs to take part in public business without an effort. Their natural bent leads them to leave public business to the one visible and permanent representative of the community’s interests, that is to say, to the state. Not only do they naturally lack a taste for public business; they often have no time for it. Private life is so busy in democratic periods, so excited, so full of wishes and of work, that hardly any energy or leisure is left to each individual for public life. I am the last man to maintain that these propensities are unconquerable, since my chief object in writing this book has been to combat them. I maintain only that at the present day a secret power is fostering them in the human heart, and that if they are not checked they will entirely overgrow it.

I have also had occasion to show how the growing love of well-being and the fluctuating character of property make democratic nations dread all violent disturbance. The love of public tranquility is often the only passion these nations keep, and it grows more active and powerful among them as all other passions droop and die. This naturally disposes the members of the community constantly to give or surrender additional rights to the central power, which alone seems to have an interest in defending them by the same means it uses to defend itself. In ages of equality no man is compelled to lend his assistance to his fellow men, and none has any right to expect much support from them. Everyone is therefore at once independent and powerless. These two conditions, which must never be considered separately or confounded together, inspire the citizen of a democratic country with very contrary tendencies. His independence fills him with self-reliance and pride among his equals. His weakness makes him feel, from time to time, the need of some outside assistance, which he cannot expect from any of them, because they are all powerless and unsympathetic. In this predicament he naturally turns his eyes to that imposing power which alone rises above the level of universal depression. His needs, and especially his desires, continually remind him of that power, until he comes at last to see it as the sole and necessary support of his own weakness. *b This may more completely explain what often happens in democratic countries, where the very men who are so impatient of superiors patiently submit to a master, showing at once their pride and their servility.

[Footnote b: In democratic communities nothing but the central power has any stability in its position or any permanence in its undertakings. All the other members of society are in ceaseless stir and transformation. Now, it is in the nature of all governments to seek constantly to enlarge their sphere of action. It is therefore almost impossible for such a government not to succeed in the end, because it acts with a fixed principle and a constant will upon men whose position, ideas and desires are in continual vacillation. It often happens that the members of the community promote the influence of the central power without intending to. Democratic ages are periods of experiment, innovation and adventure. At such times there is always a multitude of men engaged in difficult or novel undertakings, which they pursue alone, without caring about their fellow men. Such persons may be ready to admit, as a general principle, that the public authority ought not to interfere in private concerns. But as an exception to that rule, each of them craves its assistance in the particular concern he is engaged in, and tries to draw on the influence of the government for his own benefit, though he would restrict it on all other occasions. Suppose a large number of men apply this particular exception to a great variety of different purposes. The sphere of the central power then extends imperceptibly in all directions, although each of them wishes it to be limited. Thus a democratic government increases its power simply by the fact of its permanence. Time is on its side, every incident befriends it, and the passions of individuals promote it unconsciously. It may be asserted that the older a democratic community is, the more centralized its government will become.]

Men’s hatred of privilege increases as privileges become scarcer and less considerable, so that democratic passions would seem to burn most fiercely just when they have the least fuel. I have already given the reason for this phenomenon. When all conditions are unequal, no inequality is great enough to offend the eye. Yet the slightest dissimilarity is odious in the midst of general uniformity, and the more complete the uniformity, the more insupportable the sight of such a difference becomes. It is therefore natural that the love of equality should constantly increase together with equality itself, and that it should grow by what it feeds on. This never-dying, ever-rekindling hatred, which sets a democratic people against the smallest privileges, is especially favorable to the gradual concentration of all political rights in the hands of the representative of the state alone. The sovereign is necessarily and incontestably above all the citizens, so he does not excite their envy, and each of them thinks he is stripping his equals of the prerogative that he concedes to the crown. The man of a democratic age is extremely reluctant to obey his neighbor, who is his equal. He refuses to acknowledge in such a person any ability superior to his own; he mistrusts his justice and is jealous of his power; he fears and despises him; and he loves to remind him constantly of the common dependence in which both stand toward the same master. Every central power that follows its natural tendencies courts and encourages the principle of equality, for equality singularly facilitates, extends and secures the influence of a central power.

In the same way, it may be said that every central government worships uniformity. Uniformity spares it from looking into an infinite number of small details that would have to be attended to if rules were adapted to men, instead of men being indiscriminately subjected to rules. Thus the government likes what the citizens like, and naturally hates what they hate. In democratic nations these common feelings constantly unite the sovereign and every member of the community in one and the same conviction, and they establish a secret and lasting sympathy between them. The faults of the government are pardoned for the sake of its tastes. Public confidence is withdrawn only reluctantly, even in the midst of its excesses and errors, and it is restored at the first call. Democratic nations often hate those in whose hands the central power is vested, but they always love that power itself.

Thus I have reached the same conclusion by two separate paths. I have shown that the principle of equality suggests to men the idea of a single, uniform and strong government, and I have now shown that it gives them a taste for it. The nations of our age are therefore tending toward governments of this kind. The natural inclination of mind and heart draws them there, and to arrive at that result it is enough that they do not hold themselves back in their course. I am of the opinion that in the democratic ages now opening upon us, individual independence and local liberties will always be the product of artificial contrivance, and that centralization will be the natural form of government. *c
